To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the photoreceptors of the spider monkey eye are not oriented toward a point in the center of the eye but rather toward a point anterior to the center of rotation of the eye, that the orientation of the receptors is not random but is organized into groups, that the groups are organized in an alternating fashion, and that the groups are oriented so as to maximize their exposure to light.

the orientation of the retinal receptors of the spider monkey is toward an anterior point rather than to the retinal center, that the anterior point is at the fovea, and that the angular difference between neighboring photoreceptors is about the same for both the center- and anterior-pointing hypothesis.

the photoreceptors of the spider monkey eye are oriented to a point anterior to the center of a sphere of equal radius, and that the orientation of the cells is such that a greater proportion of the receptors point toward the anterior than toward the posterior of the eye.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the angular relationship between the photoreceptors and the center of the retina and the implications of this relationship for retinal function.
the angular relationships of neighboring retinal photoreceptors and the orientation of these receptors in the retina.
the angular relationship of neighboring photopigment cells and the implications of these relationships for retinal physiology.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the photoreceptors of the spider monkey eye are oriented toward the anterior point of the eye.
the anterior-pointing hypothesis is more consistent with the data than the center-pointing hypothesis.
the anterior-pointing hypothesis has more support from the evidence of the data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the orientation of retinal photoreceptors is such that they tend to point toward the center of the retina.
the anterior-pointing hypothesis fits our data better than does the center- pointing hypothesis.
the orientation of the retinal receptors is not a random phenomenon but that there is a tendency for the photoreceptors to point toward a common point in the eye.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the orientation of neighboring photoreceptor cells is not random but is highly organized.
the orientation of the receptors is not uniform, and that this orientation is not random.
the anterior-pointing hypothesis is more consistent with the data.
